## Introduction

Alkalosis refers to a primary pathophysiologic process that increases blood pH by reducing hydrogen ion concentration or increasing bicarbonate concentration. When this process results in an arterial pH greater than 7.45, the condition is termed alkalemia. This condition represents one end of the acid-base disorder spectrum. There is, in general, a loss of hydrogen ions (H+) or an excess of bicarbonate ions (HCO3-), with various factors potentially causing either of these mechanisms. Alkalosis can be as life-threatening as acidosis, and severe electrolyte derangements can accompany alkalosis due to transcellular shifts, potentially resulting in rare but severe clinical disorders. Alkalosis can originate from either respiratory or metabolic causes, with metabolic alkalosis being more common. The renal and pulmonary systems are the primary regulators of serum pH levels. Respiratory alkalosis results in compensatory metabolic acidosis, whereas metabolic alkalosis results in compensatory respiratory acidosis. However, the pH does not typically correct to the normal value of 7.40. Respiratory compensation for metabolic alkalosis occurs rapidly through hypoventilation, whereas renal compensation for respiratory alkalosis develops over several days through increased bicarbonate excretion.[1][2][3][2]

When alkalemia becomes severe (pH >7.6), it can lead to vasoconstriction, confusion or delirium, seizures, arrhythmias, and symptoms related to hypocalcemia, such as paresthesias and carpopedal spasms. Hypocalcemia occurs because elevated pH increases calcium binding to albumin, reducing ionized calcium levels. Respiratory compensation for metabolic alkalosis may lead to hypoventilation, which is usually not clinically significant. However, in patients with impaired respiratory drive, such as those with chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD) or obesity hypoventilation syndrome, severe metabolic alkalosis can further suppress ventilation and exacerbate hypercapnea or hypoxemia.[4][5]

## Etiology

The etiologies of alkalosis can be divided into metabolic and respiratory causes and are also affected by volume status and complex intracellular and intercellular interactions. Of note, patients often have multiple acid-base disorders simultaneously, and this must be taken into consideration.

A normally functioning kidney has significant capacity to regulate acid-base balance within a narrow physiologic range. Metabolic alkalosis commonly develops when an exogenous alkali load is superimposed on impaired renal bicarbonate excretion, particularly in states of reduced effective arterial blood volume, such as hypovolemia, congestive heart failure, or cirrhosis. Under these conditions, renal dysfunction and secondary hyperaldosteronism limit bicarbonate elimination and enhance distal hydrogen ion secretion, promoting bicarbonate retention.[3][6]

Exogenous alkali sources include acetate-containing total parenteral nutrition, citrate from massive transfusions or plasmapheresis, and excessive bicarbonate ingestion as seen in milk-alkali syndrome or chronic calcium carbonate use. Furthermore, ongoing gastrointestinal chloride losses, as seen in secretory diarrhea associated with villous adenomas, chronic laxative abuse, or high-volume ileostomy output, perpetuate bicarbonate retention due to impaired renal chloride delivery. In individuals with cystic fibrosis, substantial chloride loss through sweat can also contribute to metabolic alkalosis by promoting extracellular fluid contraction and secondary hyperaldosteronism, thereby enhancing renal bicarbonate reabsorption. In summary, despite the overlap between etiologies, the net effect is an increase in bicarbonate or a decrease in H+ ions, leading to metabolic alkalosis.[2][6][2][7]

I. Metabolic Alkalosis

A. Metabolic Alkalosis Mechanisms

Excess loss of hydrogen ions: This is primarily due to gastric losses—such as gastric lavage or excessive emesis of gastric contents (eg, pyloric stenosis). Gastric contents contain large amounts of chloride in the forms of hydrochloric acid (primary), sodium chloride, and potassium chloride. As part of the digestive process, the gastric parietal cells secrete hydrogen ions, which are combined with bicarbonate secreted by the small intestine. When the parietal cell hydrogen ions are lost, the secreted bicarbonate is absorbed into the extracellular compartment. This bicarbonate is then excreted by the kidneys as NaHCO3, leading to transient volume depletion.[8][9] This volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, thereby promoting potassium secretion. Hypokalemia leads to the exchange of intracellular potassium for extracellular hydrogen and increases renal ammoniagenesis and bicarbonate secretion, further propagating alkalemia. Low chloride also downregulates the HCO3-/Cl- exchanger pendrin in the distal nephron β-intercalated cells.[1]

Increased bicarbonate in the extracellular compartment: This occurs due to excess enteral intake of bicarbonate or alkali, such as in milk-alkali syndrome, or increased parenteral intake of citrate, acetate, or lactate, which can be converted to bicarbonate. Commonly ingested bicarbonate-containing medications include baking soda, sodium bicarbonate tablets, potassium bicarbonate tablets, and potassium citrate tablets. Sodium citrate is also used as an anticoagulant in fresh frozen plasma, and transfusing large volumes can lead to metabolic alkalosis.[2][7]

Increased renal reabsorption of bicarbonate: Increased renal reabsorption of bicarbonate can also contribute to metabolic alkalosis. Conditions such as primary hyperaldosteronism, renin-secreting tumors, renal artery stenosis, exogenous mineralocorticoids, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Liddle syndrome, Cushing syndrome, and Cushing disease can all act in this manner.[2]

B. Classification of Metabolic Alkalosis Causes

Metabolic alkalosis can be examined through various lenses, one of which is through the assessment of volume status.

Hypovolemic states: In general, these patients are chloride-deficient and will respond to chloride repletion.

Gastric losses: Gastric losses lead to chloride loss and volume contraction, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

Vomiting

Nasogastric tube drainage

Intestinal losses: Intestinal losses result in the loss of potassium and chloride through stool, along with fluid loss.

Ileostomy output

Villous adenoma

Some types of secretory diarrhea (stool chloride can be high)

Congenital chloridorrhea is a rare congenital disorder causing loss of the chloride/bicarbonate transporter in the distal ileum and colon, causing bicarbonate retention and impaired chloride absorption.[10]

Diuretic use:

Loop diuretics block the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle in the kidneys, reducing sodium and chloride reabsorption and increasing the excretion of water, sodium, potassium, and chloride.

Thiazide diuretics block the Na+/Cl− cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule.[2][6]

Bartter syndrome: This autosomal recessive condition is primarily caused by mutations in the NKCC2 and ROMK transporters in the thick ascending loop of Henle. Impaired Na+ reabsorption in the thick ascending loop of Henle causes excessive distal delivery of sodium, resulting in enhanced distal convoluted tubule sodium reabsorption (via the epithelial sodium channel, ENaC) and exchange with a positively charged potassium or hydrogen ion, which leads to increased loss of potassium and hydrogen in urine. In addition, loss of the electropositivity of the thick ascending loop of Henle results in the inability to reabsorb magnesium and calcium through claudin channels, leading to nephrocalcinosis. About 50% of cases present in the first year of life and can present as failure to thrive, polyuria, polydipsia, and vomiting.[11] There are 5 known variants. Please see StatPearls' companion reference, "Bartter Syndrome," for more details.

Gitelman syndrome: This autosomal recessive syndrome affects the NCC transporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Gitelman syndrome is characterized by metabolic alkalosis, renal potassium wasting, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypochloremia, and hypocalciuria. Gitelman syndrome is also referred to as familial hypokalemia-hypomagnesemia and generally presents in late childhood or adulthood.[12][13] Please see StatPearls' companion reference, "Gitelman Syndrome," for more details. The renin-aldosterone axis is highly activated in both Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, leading to hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Both Bartter and Gitelman syndromes cannot be treated with sodium and chloride repletion alone due to the respective receptor mutations causing sodium and chloride wasting.

Cystic fibrosis: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), which is crucial for chloride ion transport. Patients have thickened mucosal secretions and often have chronic respiratory acidosis from impaired CO2 exchange; however, metabolic alkalosis is also frequently documented. Downregulation of pendrin receptors (a HCO3-/Cl- exchanger) in the B intercalated cells of the collecting tubules, leading to bicarbonate retention and chloride secretion, has been demonstrated in multiple studies. The renal chloride loss and bicarbonate retention significantly exacerbate metabolic alkalosis in the context of volume depletion and can worsen respiratory acidosis.[14][15][16][15][16]

Hypervolemic states: In general, the alkalosis in these patients will not respond to chloride repletion.

Aldosterone excess, renin-secreting tumors, Cushing syndrome, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia

Increased sodium absorption in the collecting ducts results in the excretion of hydrogen and potassium. Potassium loss can worsen metabolic alkalosis by causing potassium to shift from the intracellular to the extracellular space, resulting in an intracellular hydrogen shift. Cortisol binds to aldosterone receptors with high affinity, mainly if not activated by 11-β-dehydrogenase. Defects in 11-βdehydrogenase or large amounts of natural licorice, which contains glycyrrhizic acid that inhibits this enzyme, can lead to the abovementioned symptoms.[6]

Liddle syndrome

This rare autosomal dominant condition is characterized by a gain-of-function in the epithelial sodium channel in the collecting tubule. Affected patients typically present with hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis—findings that are similar to those observed in other disorders caused by mineralocorticoid excess. Liddle syndrome is characterized by highly resistant hypertension.[17] Please see StatPearls' companion reference, "Liddle Syndrome," for more details.

Non-volume dependent: If these patients are not volume-depleted, in general, these patients will not respond to chloride repletion and often have underlying renal insufficiency (either acute or chronic) as the kidneys are usually able to regulate electrolytes within a narrow range.

Exogenous alkali administration

Excessive intake of bicarbonate (eg, via antacids or IV bicarbonate), citrate (eg, in blood transfusions), or total parenteral nutrition with excess acetate can sustain alkalosis. The kidneys may fail to excrete excess bicarbonate quickly enough, especially if renal function is impaired or if other factors (eg, hypokalemia) are present.[1]

Severe potassium depletion

Hypokalemia stimulates hydrogen ion secretion in the distal tubule and enhances bicarbonate reabsorption. Potassium depletion also increases ammonia production in the proximal tubule, which buffers hydrogen ions in the urine, further generating bicarbonate. In addition, hypokalemia activates NHE3 and basolateral NBCe1 and downregulates pendrin, further increasing alkalosis. Saline alone cannot correct this without addressing potassium deficiency.[1][6]

Post-hypercapnic alkalosis

After chronic hypercapnia (eg, in COPD), rapid correction of high CO2 levels (eg, via mechanical ventilation) leaves compensatory bicarbonate elevation unopposed. The kidneys retain bicarbonate due to chloride depletion or impaired excretion, and saline may not fully correct this without addressing chloride and potassium balance.[18]

C. Metabolic Alkalosis Progression

To have chloride-depletion metabolic alkalosis (ie, chloride-responsive), two distinct phases must occur: Initiation and Maintenance.

Initiation—the primary disturbances that elevate HCO3- levels, reduce H+, or cause loss of H+

GI Tract: Vomiting and nasogastric suction lead to volume loss. Initially, bicarbonate generated during gastric acid loss enters the circulation and may be excreted with sodium in the urine.

Kidneys: Diuretics (eg, loop or thiazide) cause H+ and Cl loss in urine, elevating HCO3- levels.[19][20]

Exogenous Alkali:

Iatrogenic HCO3-: Excessive administration of bicarbonate (eg, during intravenous therapy), especially in patients with renal impairment (who can’t excrete excess HCO3-), raises blood HCO3- and pH.

Milk-Alkali Syndrome: The overuse of calcium carbonate (eg, antacids) combined with high dairy intake increases alkali (HCO3-) absorption, leading to alkalosis, often accompanied by hypercalcemia.

Posthypercapnia:

In chronic respiratory acidosis (high CO2), the kidneys compensate by excreting H+ and retaining HCO3- to buffer pH. If hypercapnia is rapidly corrected (eg, through mechanical ventilation like intubation), CO2 levels drop quickly, but the elevated HCO3- persists temporarily, causing a transient metabolic alkalosis.[18]

Maintenance Phase—the sustaining processes that prolong the alkalemia

Volume Depletion:

Low blood volume (eg, from vomiting or diuretics) increases angiotensin II (ATII), which enhances proximal convoluted tubule reabsorption of HCO3-, and aldosterone promotes HCO3- retention in the cortical collecting duct by increasing Na+ reabsorption, K+ wasting, and H+ secretion, thereby maintaining metabolic alkalosis.

Chloride Depletion:

Low Cl- (eg, from vomiting) reduces Cl- uptake in the macula densa, activating the RAS, which further increases ATII and aldosterone, perpetuating HCO3- reabsorption.

In the cortical collecting duct, reduced Cl- availability prevents HCO3- secretion via the Cl-/HCO3- exchanger, favoring HCO3- retention in the blood.

Hypokalemia:

Enhances ammoniagenesis in proximal tubule cells, leading to new HCO3- generation

Increases proximal tubular reabsorption of filtered HCO3-

Increases HCO3- generation and absorption in the collecting duct A-intercalated cells

Decreases HCO3- secretion in the collecting duct B-intercalated cells.[6]

Hyperaldosteronism (Primary or Secondary):

Elevated aldosterone (primary from adrenal issues or secondary from volume depletion) increases cortical collecting duct α-intercalated cell H+ secretion, retaining HCO3- in the blood.

Aldosterone also drives Na+ reabsorption in principal cells, which promotes H+ secretion to maintain electrical neutrality, further reducing blood H+ and sustaining alkalosis.[19][20]

3. Compensatory Metabolic Alkalosis:

It is also worth mentioning the physiological response to chronic respiratory acidosis. In conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, obesity hypoventilation syndrome, or obstructive sleep apnea, sustained carbon dioxide retention prompts the kidneys to retain bicarbonate in order to buffer the acidosis and help maintain a near-normal blood pH. This occurs through chronic downregulation of the transporter pendrin.[1]

II. Respiratory Alkalosis:

Carbon dioxide (CO ) is a by-product of aerobic metabolism, and respiratory alkalosis is induced by a process causing hyperventilation. The hyperventilation can be due to central causes, hypoxia, cardiopulmonary disease, iatrogenic, or physiologic. Two very rare exceptions are hypothermia, where decreased CO production can result from decreased metabolism, but these are rarely encountered.[21][22][23]

As noted, hyperventilation may be due to central, hypoxemic, cardiopulmonary, iatrogenic, or physiologic causes.[24][25]

Central causes:

Head injury

Stroke

Hyperthyroidism

Anxiety

Pain

Fear

Drugs and toxins, such as salicylates, beta-agonists, and endotoxin [26][27][28]

Hypoxemic causes:

High altitude

Pulmonary disease [29][30][29]

Cardiopulmonary causes:

Pulmonary embolism

Pneumothorax

Pneumonia

Acute asthma

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbations

Cardiogenic edema [29][31]

Iatrogenic causes:

Hyperventilation in intubated patients on mechanical ventilation

Extracorporeal membranous oxygenation [29]

Physiologic causes:

Pregnancy

Hyperthermia, including fever [32][33]

Hypoxic stimulation leads to hyperventilation in an attempt to correct hypoxia at the expense of CO2 loss. Physiological causes of hyperventilation include pregnancy and fever, which increase metabolic rates and lead to hyperventilation. Another physiological cause is hyperthermia, which can increase minute ventilation and cause hypocapnia at rest and during exercise, although the exact mechanisms by which this occurs are not fully elucidated.[26][29]

Leigh syndrome is a rare, genetic neurodegenerative disorder that causes respiratory alkalosis through centrally driven hyperventilation, and the condition can be exacerbated by oxygen supplementation. This disorder typically presents in infancy or childhood, but late-onset cases have been described. Respiratory alkalosis causes compensatory lactate accumulation. Several studies have shown the adverse effects of alkalosis on the central nervous system, and alkalosis also causes cerebral vasoconstriction. Although this is a rare disease, it provides insight into the physiological effects of respiratory alkalosis, particularly on the brain.[34][35]

## Pathophysiology

The intracellular pH is between 7.0 and 7.35, making it more acidic than the extracellular blood. The extracellular and intracellular pH levels are assiduously maintained within a narrow range by active mechanisms. The body has a robust buffering system that minimizes pH changes in the initial stages of acid-base derangements. When these buffering systems are overwhelmed, alkalosis may result.[38]

The primary extracellular buffering system in the human body is the bicarbonate/carbon dioxide (HCO3/CO2) chemical equilibrium system, represented by the following equation:

H+ + HCO3− <----> H2CO3<----> CO2 + H2O [39]

This reaction is catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase. HCO3- acts as an alkalotic substance by accepting a hydrogen ion, whereas H2CO3 (carbonic acid) serves as an acidic substance by releasing a hydrogen ion. Therefore, increased bicarbonate or decreased carbon dioxide—resulting in lower H2CO3 levels—can lead to alkalemia. The opposite is also true, where a decrease in bicarbonate or an increase in carbon dioxide induces acidemia. Carbon dioxide levels are physiologically regulated by the pulmonary system through respiration, whereas bicarbonate levels are regulated by the renal system through reabsorption. Therefore, respiratory alkalosis results from a decrease in plasma CO2. Although it is theoretically possible to have decreased CO2 production, this illness almost always results from hyperventilation, where CO2 is expelled from the body.[40]

The kidneys maintain normal acid-base balance through 2 primary mechanisms—bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule and bicarbonate production in the distal nephron. About 85% to 90% of filtered bicarbonate occurs in the proximal tubule, with the remaining 10% to 15% absorbed in the thick ascending loop of Henle or distal convoluted tubule and 3% to 5% in the distal collecting duct. Although considerably less bicarbonate is absorbed in the distal nephron, this is where a significant portion of regulation and fine-tuning occurs. [6][40]

Reabsorption of bicarbonate in the proximal tubule is mediated by a Na+/H+ antiporter and the hydrogen-ATPase. The secreted hydrogen ion (H+) combines with luminal bicarbonate (HCO3-), dissociating into carbon dioxide and water, catalyzed by luminal carbonic anhydrase. Carbon dioxide enters the proximal tubular cell, where it is catalyzed by cytosolic carbonic anhydrase to produce HCO3-. This bicarbonate is then transported into the serum with sodium through the Na+/HCO3- cotransporter (NBCe1).[41]

The thick ascending loop of Henle is the location of a key regulatory channel known as the Na+/K+/2Cl −cotransporter (NKCC2). This transporter absorbs sodium, potassium, and chloride from the lumen into the blood and serves as the site of action for loop diuretics. This segment also contains the Na+/H+ exchanger 3 (NHE3), which transports sodium into the cell and the blood and secretes hydrogen into the urine. These processes are powered by the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase.[42]

Na+ and Cl −typically coexist in a ratio of 1.4:1. In metabolic alkalosis, this balance is disrupted, and chloride is secreted in exchange for bicarbonate. This regulation primarily occurs in the cortical collecting ducts. The cortical collecting ducts contain 3 cell types—type A intercalated cells, type B intercalated cells, and principal cells. The functions are as follows:

Type A intercalated cells: These cells secrete H+ through hydrogen-ATPases, generating new HCO3- by cytosolic carbonic anhydrase. This new HCO3- is transported into the blood by the basolateral HCO3-/Cl- anion exchange protein 1 (AE1).

Type B intercalated cells: These cells secrete HCO3- into the tubular lumen in exchange for luminal Cl through the apical HCO3-/Cl- exchanger called pendrin. The resultant acid is reabsorbed into the blood through the basolateral hydrogen-ATPase.

Principal cells: These cells reabsorb sodium through the epithelial sodium channel, and water is absorbed along with sodium through aquaporin 2 channels. Principal cells also secrete potassium. The primary site of action for aldosterone is in these principal cells.

Ammoniagenesis is also part of bicarbonate metabolism. Ammonia (NH3) is a weak base, and, at a physiologic pH, it can acquire H+ from H2O to become ammonium (NH4+), which is eventually secreted in the distal collecting duct type A intercalated cell through the apical hydrogen-ATPase; this antiporter is upregulated by aldosterone. Hypokalemia increases ammoniagenesis, increases the activity of the hydrogen-ATPase, and decreases the activity of type B intercalated cells in the collecting tubule.

Low potassium levels correlate with metabolic alkalosis due to increased intracellular hydrogen levels to retain electroneutrality (in exchange for transporting potassium extracellularly). When protons shift into the cellular compartment, metabolic alkalosis develops, followed by respiratory center depression of respiratory drive. Intracellular acidosis also stimulates ammoniagenesis (via glutamine metabolism) in the proximal tubule, further increasing H+ loss. A cycle develops whereby alkalosis promotes an intracellular shift of potassium, predisposing to hypokalemia, and increases calcium binding to albumin, lowering ionized calcium levels and occasionally causing neuromuscular irritability.[43][44][43]

Acute and Chronic Metabolic Compensation for Respiratory Alkalosis

In the acute phase, intracellular and extracellular buffers release hydrogen ions to mitigate the deficit, resulting in a modest reduction in plasma bicarbonate of ~2 mEq/L for every 10 mm Hg decrease in PaCO2.[45]

With chronic respiratory alkalosis, the kidneys adapt over several days primarily by downregulating ammoniagenesis and reducing net acid excretion, with a secondary reduction in proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption. This results in increased bicarbonate excretion and minimized hydrogen ion loss.[46] The steady-state decrease in bicarbonate is approximately 4 to 5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg fall in PaCO2.

Respiratory Acidosis Compensation for Metabolic Alkalosis

Conversely, respiratory depression resulting in increased PaCO occurs promptly and predictably to buffer the alkalemia resulting from metabolic conditions. Although exact values may vary, expectations are that there is a 0.6-0.7 mm Hg increase in PaCO per 1 mmol/L increase in HCO2. Alkalemia also causes a shift in the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve towards the left, thus increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen and decreasing oxygen release to the tissues.[47]

Physiologic Consequences: Alkalemia shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the left, enhancing hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen and thereby reducing tissue oxygen delivery. In addition, alkalosis promotes an intracellular shift of potassium, predisposing to hypokalemia, and increases calcium binding to albumin, lowering ionized calcium levels and occasionally causing neuromuscular irritability [43].

## History and Physical

A comprehensive evaluation of metabolic alkalosis begins with a systematic assessment of volume status, electrolyte abnormalities, and underlying causes, integrating both clinical findings and historical clues.

Alkalosis can present with a wide range of signs and symptoms depending on the etiology (respiratory versus metabolic) and the underlying primary condition. In metabolic alkalosis, history may include vomiting, diarrhea, known endocrine disorders, licorice ingestion, or hypertension of unknown cause. In respiratory alkalosis, the history may include mechanical ventilation, trauma, central line catheter insertion, recent surgery, thromboembolic disease, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, aspirin ingestion, or a central neurological process.

A meticulous medication review is particularly essential: diuretics, antacids, sodium bicarbonate, or citrate-containing transfusions as potential sources of exogenous alkali should be identified.[48]

Symptoms may include dyspnea, fever, chills, peripheral edema, orthopnea, weakness, confusion, light-headedness, dizziness, anxiety, chest pain, numbness, paresthesia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or tinnitus. Patients with respiratory alkalosis can have associated syncope, tremors, and signs of hyperventilation, along with chest pain and dyspnea.

The primary sign of respiratory alkalosis is an increased respiratory rate. Although a normal respiratory rate is often defined as 20 breaths/minute, a normal adult respiratory rate is 12 to 16 breaths/minute, and there is some evidence that this increases with age.[49]

Metabolic alkalosis can present with a variety of systemic manifestations:

-Neurologic: Symptoms result from reduced ionized calcium (reflecting neuromuscular irritability from hypocalcemia in the setting of alkalosis) and cerebral vasoconstriction, ranging from confusion, agitation, and lethargy to seizures or coma. Peripheral findings may include paresthesias, tremors, muscle cramps, twitching, and positive Trousseau or Chvostek signs. -Musculoskeletal: Muscle weakness is common, especially with coexistent hypokalemia. -Cardiovascular: Arrhythmias may occur due to hypokalemia and hypocalcemia. -Normochloremic metabolic alkalosis typically correlates with hypertension and volume expansion, often reflecting mineralocorticoid excess states.[6]

Volume Status: Determining volume status and whether the alkalosis is saline-responsive or saline-resistant is a cornerstone of evaluation. Mitigating factors may include a history of vomiting, nasogastric suction, or diuretic use, all of which cause chloride and volume depletion, leading to increased renal bicarbonate reabsorption. In volume contraction (saline-responsive), urinary chloride is typically low (<20 mmol/L) unless a diuretic is present.[36] Hypovolemia may be suggested by hypotension, tachycardia, dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, or orthostatic changes.

Pediatric Considerations

In infants and children, failure to thrive, polyuria, polydipsia, and vomiting should raise suspicion for Bartter or Gitelman syndromes. -These inherited tubulopathies are rare and can be easily missed. -A detailed family history may help identify hereditary patterns. -Cystic fibrosis, which typically shows low urine chloride levels, should be differentiated from Bartter or Gitelman syndromes, which are characterized by high urine chloride levels.

-Another specific example of which to be alert is persistent and projectile, non-bilious emesis in a 2- to 6-week-old, otherwise well-appearing infant, which is a hallmark presentation of pyloric stenosis. In addition, evidence shows that infants with metabolic alkalosis who undergo surgery to fix the pyloric stenosis are more likely to have perioperative complications than those without metabolic alkalosis.[50]

Note on Respiratory Alkalosis

While evaluating metabolic alkalosis, it is useful to recognize respiratory alkalosis, which may coexist or confound interpretation. -The earliest sign is increased respiratory rate due to hyperventilation, leading to excessive CO2 washout. -This is common in anxiety, sepsis, hypoxemia, pregnancy, or chronic pulmonary disease with acute exacerbation.[36]
